description:
Take Control – A Ramadan Prayer

English & Urdu | SufiPulse USA

Ramadan is not only a month of fasting.
It is a sacred interruption.

A pause in time.
A recalibration of the heart.
A system reset for the soul.

“Take Control – A Ramadan Prayer” is a bilingual spiritual reflection presented in English and Urdu, inviting the listener beyond ritual into surrender.

This song explores Ramadan as more than hunger.
It is exposure.
It is alignment.
It is discipline that prepares the heart for revelation.

From fasting (Ṣawm) to night prayers (Tarāwīḥ), from the descent of the Qur’an to the mystery of Laylat al-Qadr, this work reflects on the architecture of reset embedded within the month.

“Take Control” is not a demand for power.
It is a plea to be freed from ego — so that what governs the heart is not impulse, but intention.

Ramadan Mubarak means “Blessed Ramadan.”
But blessing is not automatic.
It is received when the heart allows itself to be rewritten.

This song is offered as a reflection on:

• The deeper grades of fasting
• Night as intimacy, not performance
• Laylat al-Qadr as divine recalibration
• Ramadan as a state that continues beyond the month

For the seeker, Ramadan is not seasonal.
It is structural.

Let Ramadan take control.
Allow yourself to be reset.

From America, this is offered to every heart seeking renewal this Ramadan.

—

description:

The lyrics move quietly from fear to love, from “I” to silence, from seeking to being. There is no argument here, no instruction. Only a gentle dismantling.

Sufism in this song is not a title.
It is a state of the heart.

Listen without rushing.
Let the pauses speak.

title: SufiPulse Studio I Nazar e karam kar de Thori si to lift kar de (A Prayer for Inner Elevation)
description:
This is not a rebuttal of old prayers, " Lift Karadey" it’s a refinement of intention. The song respects the instinct to ask, but gently turns the direction of the asking. From wanting more to becoming right. From external lift to inner alignment. From desire shaped by the world to correction shaped by the Divine.

It doesn’t shame the earlier prayer. It completes it. That’s why the redirection is gentle. Because hearts don’t turn by force, they turn by understanding.

The song begins with a familiar prayer. A request for mercy, grace, and relief. But as it unfolds, the meaning of the “lift” quietly changes.

This is not a call for wealth or status.
It is a call for inner elevation.

The lyrics move inward, asking for peace of the heart, humility of the ego, light for the soul, patience in hardship, and trust in restraint. What starts as a plea becomes a transformation.

Rooted in devotion and Sufi thought, the song reminds us that the real rise in life is not material, but spiritual.

Listen with stillness.
The lift happens within.

description:

Main Hoon Sufi Researcher | Kainaat Ki Ayat Reader
A Sufi Reflection for Those Who Study the World

This is not a devotional song. This is not a lecture.
This is a reflection for researchers, scholars, analysts, and thinkers who spend their lives studying systems, patterns, forces, and laws.

You examine particles, organisms, equations, data sets, and cosmic structures. But rarely are you invited to examine the observer doing the examining.

This song speaks to that missing dimension.

It explores a simple but uncomfortable idea:
that every investigation of the universe is also an investigation of the self.

Science measures phenomena.
Sufism asks who is measuring.

Modern research perfected method, precision, and abstraction.
But in doing so, it often separated logic from meaning, observation from consciousness, data from inner clarity.
This separation limits insight.

Sufism does not oppose science.
It repairs the fracture within it.

Through poetry, sound, and reflection, this piece invites researchers to consider:

how intention shapes interpretation
how inner stillness affects perception
how wonder fuels discovery
how meaning begins where data ends

The lyrics trace a journey from measurement to mercy, from equation to awareness, from external analysis to inner recognition.

The slides address what is often missing in modern inquiry:
the vertical axis of mind, soul, origin, and purpose.

This is not a call to abandon science.
It is a call to recognize the mysticism already hidden inside it.

When inquiry turns inward, research changes.
When the observer becomes clear, patterns emerge.
When wonder returns, discovery deepens.

Some read the signs in cosmic orbits.
Some read them in the veins of being.
Some saw them in the riverbed.
Some in the depth of the self.

The destination was always the same.

The Lord was always near.
It was the distance within us that needed closing.

If you are a researcher who has ever felt that something essential was missing from your work, this reflection is for you.

Just listen.
Beyond belief.
Into understanding.

description:
Ya Dost (Asma se Qalb Tak) is a reflective spiritual composition that explores the relationship between the Divine Names (Asma) and the human heart (Qalb).

The song does not attempt to explain theology.
It reflects on how names shape responsibility,
and how, beyond names, relationship shapes the soul.

Each verse moves through Divine Attributes not as labels to be spoken lightly, but as qualities that demand ethical weight, inner discipline, and lived sincerity.

This work is a single composition presented in two connected parts.
Both parts together complete the meaning.
Listening to only one part gives an incomplete experience.

Please listen to Part One and Part Two in sequence.

Why “Ya Dost”

The phrase “Ya Dost” is used here as poetic address, not as a theological claim and not as a replacement for the Asma al-Husna.

It reflects a devotional tone found across classical Sufi poetry, where closeness is expressed through metaphor, not definition.

Creed remains intact.
Poetry expresses devotion.

The song makes a clear distinction:

Names define belief
Relationship reveals intention

This work is not meant to provoke debate.
It is meant to invite introspection.

title: SufiPusle Studio  I  Haji Naam Mila, Par Badla Kya ? I The Journey Ended. Did the Ego?
description:
This song is not a rejection of Hajj.
It is a reflection on what is expected to change after it.

Titles don’t humble.
 Names don’t purify.
 Only meeting yourself does

A journey completed.
 A meeting was missed.

Hajj is sacred.
The Kaaba is sacred.
The journey itself is beyond question.

But character still remains accountable.

This song was written after witnessing a recurring pattern:
people returning from pilgrimage with a title,
but without visible inner transformation.

Arguments continued.
Abuse remained.
Corruption went on.
And yet moral authority was assumed.

This work does not judge who went.
It questions what returned.

Hajj was never meant to decorate identity.
It was meant to dismantle it.

The Kaaba is not stone.
It is a mirror.

Some never went to Mecca, yet lived their entire lives bowed in humility.
Some went many times and returned quieter, softer, more careful.
And some returned unchanged, hiding behind a sacred name.

This song addresses that tension gently, firmly, honestly.

It is not an attack.
It is an invitation to self-audit.

If the body traveled, but the heart remained untouched,
the journey may still be unfinished.

Listen without defense.
Reflect without comparison.
What you see here is meant for you alone.

title: SufiPusle Studio  I  Zair-o-Zabar ka Jalwa | Qira’at-e-Qur’an That Outlived the Fire
description:
This is not a historical defense.
It is a moral mirror.

“Zair–Zabar” explores a difficult paradox in Islamic history:
how Divine preservation sometimes unfolds through flawed human instruments.

Hajjaj ibn Yusuf (c. 661–714 CE)
A Journey the Divine Allowed, Not the Man

From the siege and burning of Mecca
to the institutional standardization of Qur’anic recitation (Zair–Zabar),
this is one of the most unsettling paradoxes in Islamic history.

Mecca was attacked.
Walls were shaken.
But meaning remained untouched.

The Qur’an survived not only through devotion, but through precision, structure, and discipline. The diacritical system of zair–zabar preserved pronunciation, meaning, and transmission across regions and generations.

At the level of invention stood Abu al-Aswad al-Duʾali (RH) , a teacher and grammarian whose work depended on fragile human chains.

At the level of institutional enforcement stood Hajjaj ibn Yusuf , a figure of authority, severity, and deep controversy.

This work does not justify violence.
It does not sanctify power.

It asks a harder question:

If even fire could not erase meaning,
what have we erased through neglect?

The song turns inward 
from stone to heart,
from Mecca to the inner Mecca.

Many of us did not burn it with fire,
but with delay, ego, comfort, and indifference.

History records the fire.
Revelation preserved the breath.

🎶 ABOUT THE COMPOSITION

Language: Urdu (classical form)
Presentation: English contextual framing
Theme: Qur’anic preservation, inner accountability, Divine wisdom
Nature: Reflective, spiritual, non-commercial

🤲 CLOSING PRAYER (FROM THE SONG)

O Allah,
we burned our inner home.
We abandoned our inner Mecca.
Restore us the way You preserve meaning
with mercy, not illusion.
Ameen.

title: “Needle to Noor | سادۂ نجات | Saada-e-Najaat” ( Voice for the Mubtala, the one caught in addiction)
description:
“Needle to Noor” is not just a song.
It is a voice for the Mubtala , the one caught in drug addiction, and a reminder that life is more important than ego, shame, or reputation.

Addiction across Kashmir and the broader world is no longer a hidden issue.
Young lives are slipping away in silence while families struggle between fear and stigma. 

This song was created because the conversations around addiction are still filled with judgment, secrecy, and hesitation, when what people truly need is clarity, support, and dignity. SufiPulse has addressed addiction once before in its early months. Today, with stronger resources, deeper understanding, and a larger community, we return to this subject with more honesty and responsibility.

This song gives voice to those who cannot speak for themselves.
It carries the story of pain, the cost of silence, and the call for return.

For the first time, Dr. Zarf-e-Noori , Writer, Lyricist, Composer, and Music Director,  has sung his own words, a decision shaped by personal grief. Years ago, he lost someone close to addiction. This song stands as his remembrance, and his promise that no one else should be lost quietly.

“Needle to Noor” is a Sufi responsibility, because a Sufi does not only worship God; a Sufi serves humanity. Life Is More Important Than Ego, Shame, or Reputation. Life is the only thing that cannot be replaced. Ego delays help. Shame silences the truth. Reputation can be rebuilt. Life cannot. A responsible society chooses life first. If we value life above our ego, shame, and reputation, we save people before they fall too far.

This is our contribution, our solidarity, and our Saada-e-Najaat
for every youth trying to step out of darkness and every family holding on to hope.

If this song reaches you, stay with it till the last line. Sharing it may become your contribution to someone’s return.

description:
This kalam is a call from the heart toward the one who spent his life pointing humanity back to Allah Ghaus-ul-Azam Sayyid Abdul Qadir Jilani (Rahmatullah Alayh). The piece blends devotion, scholarship, and sound design to revive the spiritual practice of calling upon the beloved servants of God for help, while keeping the heart anchored firmly in Tawheed.

This project is rooted in the authentic Islamic tradition. The Prophet ﷺ himself taught tawassul. A blind man came seeking healing; the Prophet ﷺ told him to make wudu’, pray two rak‘ahs, and say: “O Allah, I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy. O Muhammad, I turn through you to my Lord for my need. O Allah, accept his intercession for me.” — Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ahmad (authentic hadith). The companions continued this practice after the Prophet ﷺ’s passing. Sayyiduna Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) said during a drought: “We used to seek rain through our Prophet ﷺ. Now we seek it through al-‘Abbas, the uncle of our Prophet.” — Sahih al-Bukhari (1010)

The help is always from Allah. The waseelah is love.

A true Sufi never mistakes the direction for the destination. Calling upon Ghaus-e-Azam is turning your heart toward a servant who never stopped pointing people toward the One.

description:
This song is carried by the verse of Nyam Saeb (Nyam Sahib, 1782–1854) — known as the Sufi Shair-e-Muntazir and a spiritual transmitter of Kashmir.

Nyam Saeb a voice of love that stretched beyond limits, breaking all measures of longing. Nyam Saeb’s poetry is not gentle yearning; it is a storm. His love runs so deep that it shatters the self, tears away the veils, and dares to stand in the fire of the Beloved.

In his verses, Nyam Saeb speaks from a place where reason collapses. He walks the razor’s edge where few have dared to go,  surrendering identity, time, and even language itself. His depth is such that his poems read like cries torn from the soul in its final undoing.

Nyam Saeb’s annihilation was not disappearance but awareness itself — a soul that waited, listened, and lived only in God. His love ran so deep it stripped the self bare, daring to step beyond reason into pure longing. Shamas Faqir (the Yunus Emre of Kashmir) would later flow as a river springing from Soch Kral’s source — but Nyam Saeb’s voice was the storm before the river.

title: Mansoor! Jala! Mita! Bana! Saja!
description:
Jala! Mita! Bana! Saja!  Burn falsehood, Erase the ego, Create truth, Adorn the soul.

Performed in URDU , with multi-subtitles available in Roman Urdu, English, Arabic, Farsi, Spanish, Hindi, Turkish, Bengali, Punjabi, and Indonesian for global seekers

A high-energy Sufi anthem honoring Mansoor al-Hallaj, the martyr whose cry Ana al-Haqq (“I am the Truth”) still shakes the heavens. This performance unfolds his journey  from the fire of truth that entered his soul, to the ashes where his being dissolved, from the chains that forged the star of knowledge, to the blood that dyed the flag of truth.

Who Was Mansoor al-Hallaj?
Mansoor al-Hallaj (858–922 CE) was a Persian Sufi mystic, poet, and teacher known for his fearless declaration Ana al-Haqq — “I am the Truth.” In Sufi understanding, this was not a claim of personal divinity but a statement of complete annihilation of the ego (fana) and total union with God (baqa).

Why Was He Punished?
His words challenged the religious and political authorities of his time. Accused of heresy, Mansoor was imprisoned for years, publicly flogged, mutilated, and finally executed in Baghdad. Even as his body suffered, his spirit remained steadfast in love for the Divine. His blood, in Sufi symbolism, became the “dye” that colored the flag of truth.

The Flag for Seekers
In this song, the “flag” represents the eternal mission of every seeker: to raise the banner of divine love and truth, regardless of the cost. Mansoor’s sacrifice reminds us that truth is often paid for in pain — but once raised, the flag never falls. Every era has its “Mansoor” who carries it forward.

About the Song
This high-energy Sufi anthem narrates Mansoor’s journey in 7 powerful verses, from the moment divine fire touched his soul, to the ashes of his body, to the rebirth of love in every age. The repeated chorus — Jala! Mita! Bana! Saja! — calls on seekers to burn falsehood, erase the ego, create truth, and adorn the soul.


About the Writer, Lyricist & Composer — Zarf-e-Noori
Zarf-e-Noori is a Kashmiri American creative force whose work blends the depth of Sufi mysticism with the precision of a modern thinker. As a writer, lyricist, and composer, he crafts verses that move between spiritual devotion, poetic beauty, and social awakening.

His lyrical style is rooted in centuries-old Kashmiri and Islamic heritage, yet it speaks in a voice that resonates with today’s global audience. Whether in qawwali, chant, or anthem, every line is written to stir the soul, awaken reflection, and carry the listener toward truth.

Beyond the pen and melody, Zarf-e-Noori is also a Remote Sensing Interpreter, Environmental Scientist, Emergency Planner, SaaS Developer, and Entrepreneur — skills that enrich his writing with both grounded knowledge and visionary perspective.
